as_told: Hippasus of Metapontum, a member of the Pythagorean school, proved that some lengths, such as the square root of 2, cannot be written as a ratio of whole numbers. This broke the Pythagorean belief that all is number. To keep the secret, the other Pythagoreans threw him overboard from a ship and drowned him.
lesson: The discovery of irrational numbers was so threatening to Greek mathematics that the Pythagoreans suppressed it by force.
what_happened: No ancient source that I read says that the Pythagoreans killed anyone. Iamblichus, who died before 333 AD, gives several versions. In one, Hippasus 'perished in the sea, as an impious person' for revealing how to form a sphere from twelve pentagons (the dodecahedron), not for irrationals. In another, the man who revealed the theory of commensurable and incommensurable quantities was expelled and given a tomb as if dead; others said the divine power punished him at sea. Pappus's commentary on Book X of Euclid, which does not name Hippasus, reports only a saying that the first person to reveal irrationals 'perished by drowning', and calls it 'most probably a parable'. The version in which shipmates throw him overboard appears in modern books.
false_part: The ancient sources do not say that the Pythagoreans drowned Hippasus; they say he died at sea as a punishment by the gods, or that the revealer of irrationals was expelled, and one source calls the drowning a parable.

earliest_telling.who: Iamblichus, On the Pythagoric Life, ch. 18 (section 88), in the English translation by Thomas Taylor, 1818. This is the earliest surviving telling of a death at sea, not of a killing by the Pythagoreans for irrationals.
earliest_telling.where: Iamblichus' Life of Pythagoras, or Pythagoric Life, translated by Thomas Taylor (London, 1818)
earliest_telling.quote: he perished in the sea, as an impious person, but obtained the renown of having made the discovery

original.what: Iamblichus, On the Pythagoric Life, ch. 34 (sections 246-247), Taylor's translation: the revealer of incommensurables was expelled and given a tomb
original.quote: constructed a tomb for him, as one who had migrated from the human

original.what: Same passage: the death at sea is credited to divine anger, and tied by some to the dodecahedron and by others to irrationals
original.quote: But according to others, this happened to him who unfolded the doctrine of irrational and incommensurable quantities.

original.what: Pappus, Commentary on Book X of Euclid's Elements, Part I, section 2, in the English translation from the Arabic by William Thomson, 1930
original.quote: perished by drowning: which is most probably a parable

lesson_verdict.why: The historian of Greek mathematics Wilbur Knorr called the 'foundations crisis' a modern fiction: he found no sign that geometers held back from using proportions in the years 450 to 350 BC, and pointed to the works of Hippocrates and Archytas, which depend on them.

source.what: Wilbur R. Knorr, The impact of modern mathematics on ancient mathematics (lecture given in 1975), Revue d'histoire des mathématiques 7 (2001), pp. 121-135
source.quote: The works of Hippocrates and Archytas, for instance, are indispensably based on such techniques.

search_steps: Read the English Wikipedia article on Hippasus as a lead: it cites Iamblichus (sections 88, 246-247), Pappus (Thomson 1930, p. 64), and modern retellings by Kline (1990) and Singh (1998).

Saved Thomas Taylor's 1818 translation of Iamblichus from archive.org (b29318610). Section 88 ties the death at sea to the dodecahedron; sections 246-247 give the expulsion and tomb, and the divine punishment at sea.
Taylor's footnotes point to the first scholium on Book X of Euclid in Commandino's 1572 edition; I did not obtain that scholium.
Saved Pappus's commentary on Book X (Thomson 1930) from archive.org. It reports the drowning as a saying and a probable parable, and does not name Hippasus.

Open Library full-text search for Hippasus overboard: earliest dated hit is Introduction to the theory of numbers, catalogue year 1983 (archive.org introductiontoth00haro), snippet only; the book is lending-only.
Open Library full-text search for Hippasus drowned irrational: hits include Studies in Presocratic Philosophy (catalogue year 1970), snippet only, lending-only.

Open Library searches for Hippasus with "thrown into the sea" and "drowned him": the only readable full text is Graeber, The Utopia of Rules (2015); earlier books are lending-only. I found no readable modern telling earlier than 2015, so I did not quote one.
Web search for scholarship on the alleged crisis over irrationals: found Knorr's 1975 lecture, published open access on Numdam in 2001; saved it.
Burkert, Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972), and von Fritz (1945) are not readable online; not used.
confidence_note: The Pappus commentary survives only in Arabic, so the wording is a translation of a translation. The Euclid scholium was not read. I could not find the first modern book that says the Pythagoreans threw Hippasus overboard; the earliest dated hit I saw is a 1983 catalogue year, snippet only. The ancient sources cannot show whether Hippasus died at sea at all.
